authors: Johannes Haushofer and Jeremy Shapiro
finding: Unconditional cash transfers raised average monthly household consumption from 158 to 193 PPP dollars nine months after the transfers began.
title: The Short-term Impact of Unconditional Cash Transfers to the Poor: Experimental Evidence from Kenya
why: Giving poor households money directly, with no conditions, quickly lifts the most basic measure of material welfare.

authors: Edward Miguel and Michael Kremer
finding: School based deworming in Kenya cut school absenteeism by one quarter, and the health gains spilled over to untreated children in nearby schools.
title: Worms: Identifying Impacts on Education and Health in the Presence of Treatment Externalities
why: Some floor level goods, like basic child health, are so cheap and so full of spillovers that they should be funded for everyone.

authors: Edward P. Lazear
finding: When the Safelite Glass Corporation moved workers to piece rates, output per worker rose by 44 percent.
title: Performance Pay and Productivity
why: How you pay people changes what they produce, so any shared system must design its rewards with care.

authors: Karthik Muralidharan and Venkatesh Sundararaman
finding: After two years, students in schools where teachers earned bonuses averaging 3 percent of pay scored 0.27 standard deviations higher in math and 0.17 higher in language than students in control schools.
title: Teacher Performance Pay: Experimental Evidence from India
why: Small, well aimed incentives can raise public service quality for the poor at very low cost.

authors: Martina Björkman and Jakob Svensson
finding: One year after communities began monitoring local health clinics with citizen report cards, deaths among children under five were 33 percent lower in treatment communities.
title: Power to the People: Evidence from a Randomized Field Experiment on Community-Based Monitoring in Uganda
why: Organized citizen oversight, with no new funding, can make public services answer to the people they serve.

authors: Benjamin A. Olken
finding: Raising the chance of a government audit on village road projects from 4 percent to 100 percent cut missing expenditures by about 8 percentage points.
title: Monitoring Corruption: Evidence from a Field Experiment in Indonesia
why: Credible, announced verification changes behavior before any punishment, which is the working core of a trust based commons.

authors: Raj Chetty and co-authors
finding: The gap in life expectancy between the richest 1 percent and the poorest 1 percent was 14.6 years for men and 10.1 years for women.
title: The Association Between Income and Life Expectancy in the United States, 2001-2014
why: It prices the floor in years of life, the only currency that counts at the base.

authors: Hannah Arem and co-authors
finding: In 661,137 adults, even activity below the recommended weekly minimum came with a 20 percent lower risk of death, and 1 to 2 times the minimum came with a 31 percent lower risk.
title: Leisure Time Physical Activity and Mortality: A Detailed Pooled Analysis of the Dose-Response Relationship
why: Movement is free and needs no clinic, so it is a health lever within everyone's reach at once.

authors: Matthew A. Killingsworth and Daniel T. Gilbert
finding: In about 250,000 sampled moments from 2,250 adults, minds were wandering 46.9 percent of the time, and people were less happy while wandering than while present, whatever they were doing.
title: A Wandering Mind Is an Unhappy Mind
why: Nearly half of waking life is spent mentally elsewhere and poorer for it, so tools that gently return attention to the present serve almost everyone.

authors: Daniel Kahneman and Angus Deaton
finding: In more than 450,000 survey responses, emotional well-being rose with income up to about 75,000 dollars a year and then stopped rising, even though life evaluation kept rising with income.
note: Added at build to complete the domain after a duplicate was removed.
title: High income improves evaluation of life but not emotional well-being
venue: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences
why: It marks the point where money stops buying daily peace of mind, which is why raising incomes below it does such deep work.

authors: Patrick L. Hill and Nicholas A. Turiano
finding: Each standard deviation rise in reported purpose in life came with a 15 percent lower risk of death over the 14 years that followed, at every adult age.
title: Purpose in Life as a Predictor of Mortality Across Adulthood
why: A reason to get up is measurable protection, not a luxury.

authors: Corey L. M. Keyes
finding: Only 17.2 percent of United States adults aged 25 to 74 met the criteria for flourishing, while 12.1 percent were languishing, and languishing adults faced nearly six times the risk of a major depressive episode that flourishing adults faced.
title: The Mental Health Continuum: From Languishing to Flourishing in Life
venue: Journal of Health and Social Behavior
why: The goal is not merely fewer people ill, but more people flourishing, and that gap can be counted.

authors: Scott Freeman and co-authors
finding: Across 225 studies, average examination scores rose by about 6 percent under active learning, and students in traditional lecture classes were 1.5 times more likely to fail.
title: Active Learning Increases Student Performance in Science, Engineering, and Mathematics
venue: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences
why: Teaching that asks learners to act, not just listen, lifts the bottom of the class most.

authors: Henry L. Roediger III and Jeffrey D. Karpicke
finding: One week after learning a passage, students who studied it once and took three recall tests remembered 61 percent of it, while students who studied it four times remembered 40 percent.
title: Test-Enhanced Learning: Taking Memory Tests Improves Long-Term Retention
why: Free recall practice costs nothing and beats rereading, a learning basic tool anyone can use anywhere.

authors: Daniel M. Oppenheimer
finding: Readers rated the author of a text rewritten with shorter, simpler words as more intelligent (4.80 versus 4.26 on a 7 point scale) than the author of the same text written with needlessly long words.
title: Consequences of Erudite Vernacular Utilized Irrespective of Necessity: Problems with Using Long Words Needlessly
why: Plain words do not cost the writer standing, they earn it.

authors: Terry C. Davis and co-authors
finding: Patients reading at or below the sixth grade level were 3.4 times less likely to interpret prescription warning labels correctly, and short single step instructions were understood better by readers at every level.
title: Low Literacy Impairs Comprehension of Prescription Drug Warning Labels
why: When a label fails, the failure sits in the wording, not the reader.

authors: Shakked Noy and Whitney Zhang
domain: Artificial intelligence and human computer interaction
finding: In a preregistered experiment with 453 professionals, access to ChatGPT cut average time on writing tasks by 40 percent and raised output quality by 18 percent, and the gap between stronger and weaker workers shrank.
title: Experimental Evidence on the Productivity Effects of Generative Artificial Intelligence
why: A shared AI tool narrowed the distance between the best and the rest.

authors: Erik Brynjolfsson, Danielle Li, and Lindsey R. Raymond
domain: Artificial intelligence and human computer interaction
finding: Among 5,179 customer support agents, an AI assistant raised issues resolved per hour by 14 percent on average and by 34 percent for novice and low skilled workers, with minimal change for the most experienced.
title: Generative AI at Work
why: The largest gains went to the people at the bottom of the skill ladder, because the tool carried the know how of top workers to everyone.

authors: Julianne Holt-Lunstad, Timothy B. Smith, and J. Bradley Layton
finding: Across 148 studies covering 308,849 people, those with stronger social relationships had a 50 percent greater likelihood of survival, an effect the authors rank alongside quitting smoking.
title: Social Relationships and Mortality Risk: A Meta-analytic Review
why: Connection is not decoration on top of the floor of a life, it is part of the floor itself.

authors: Sheldon Cohen and co-authors
finding: In a controlled virus exposure experiment with 276 volunteers, people with only 1 to 3 types of social ties had an adjusted relative risk of 4.2 for catching a cold compared with people with 6 or more types of ties.
title: Social Ties and Susceptibility to the Common Cold
why: A controlled experiment shows that widening a person's circle of ties changes their body, not just their mood.

authors: Ernst Fehr and Simon Gächter
finding: Among 240 players in a public goods game, 84.3 percent paid their own money to punish free riders at least once, and cooperation rose steadily when punishment was allowed.
title: Altruistic Punishment in Humans
why: A group can police its own fairness without a boss, because ordinary members will bear a small cost to keep the shared deal honest.

authors: Devesh Rustagi, Stefanie Engel, and Michael Kosfeld
finding: Across 49 self governing forest user groups in Ethiopia, a group where 60 percent of members were conditional cooperators spent about 14 more hours a month patrolling than a group with none, and such groups kept more potential crop trees per hectare.
title: Conditional Cooperation and Costly Monitoring Explain Success in Forest Commons Management
why: Communities left to govern their own commons protect it when enough members cooperate on condition that others do too.

authors: Soroush Vosoughi, Deb Roy, and Sinan Aral
finding: Tracking about 126,000 story cascades shared by some 3 million people on Twitter, the team found false stories were 70 percent more likely to be retweeted than true ones and reached 1,500 people about six times faster.
title: The Spread of True and False News Online
why: Truth does not win by default, so shared knowledge needs deliberate design and verification.

authors: Thomas Wood and Ethan Porter
finding: In five experiments with more than 10,100 subjects across 52 contested issues, the researchers found zero factual corrections that made people believe a falsehood more strongly.
title: The Elusive Backfire Effect: Mass Attitudes' Steadfast Factual Adherence
why: Plainly stated facts, offered to everyone, move people toward accuracy even on the questions they care about most.

authors: David Tilman, Christian Balzer, Jason Hill, Belinda L. Befort
finding: Global crop demand is forecast to rise by 100 to 110 percent between 2005 and 2050.
title: Global food demand and the sustainable intensification of agriculture
venue: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences
why: A commons that raises the floor has to plan for food demand roughly doubling while pushing yields up on land already farmed, rather than clearing new land.

authors: Emily S. Cassidy, Paul C. West, James S. Gerber, Jonathan A. Foley
finding: Growing crops only for direct human consumption could raise available food calories by up to 70 percent and feed an additional 4 billion people.
title: Redefining agricultural yields: from tonnes to people nourished per hectare
why: The floor can rise a long way by changing how existing crops are used, not only by growing more.

authors: Lorna Fewtrell, Rachel B. Kaufmann, David Kay, Wayne Enanoria, Laurence Haller, John M. Colford Jr.
finding: Across 46 studies, water, sanitation, and hygiene interventions cut diarrhoea risk, with relative risk estimates between 0.63 and 0.75.
title: Water, sanitation, and hygiene interventions to reduce diarrhoea in less developed countries: a systematic review and meta-analysis
why: Clean water, toilets, and handwashing are basic floor goods with proven health gains that a commons can deliver at community scale.

authors: Guy Hutton, Laurence Haller, Jamie Bartram
finding: In developing regions, each 1 US dollar invested in water and sanitation returned between 5 and 46 US dollars, depending on the intervention.
title: Global cost-benefit analysis of water supply and sanitation interventions
why: Money spent on water and sanitation pays for itself many times over in time saved and illness avoided, which gives a commons a hard economic case for funding it.

authors: Tim Aubry, Paula Goering, Scott Veldhuizen, Carol E. Adair, Jimmy Bourque, Jino Distasio, and coauthors
finding: Over two years, Housing First participants were in stable housing 71 percent of the time, compared with 29 percent for people receiving treatment as usual.
title: A Multiple-City RCT of Housing First With Assertive Community Treatment for Homeless Canadians With Serious Mental Illness
why: Giving people a home first, without preconditions, is a working way to lift the most exposed people off the street.

authors: Philippa Howden-Chapman, Anna Matheson, Julian Crane, Helen Viggers, Malcolm Cunningham, and coauthors
finding: People in insulated homes in low income New Zealand communities had half the odds of reporting fair or poor health, an adjusted odds ratio of 0.50.
title: Effect of insulating existing houses on health inequality: cluster randomised study in the community
why: Fixing the homes people already live in is a direct health intervention, so warm and dry housing belongs in the floor.

authors: Taryn Dinkelman
finding: In rural South Africa, household electrification raised female employment by 9 to 9.5 percentage points within five years.
title: The Effects of Rural Electrification on Employment: New Evidence from South Africa
why: Basic power frees women from home work and opens paid work, so energy belongs at the base of a shared floor.

authors: Michaël Aklin, Patrick Bayer, S. P. Harish, Johannes Urpelainen
finding: In rural India, solar microgrids raised household electrification by 29 to 36 percentage points within a year but added only 0.99 to 1.42 hours of power a day and gave no clear gain in work or study.
title: Does basic energy access generate socioeconomic benefits? A field experiment with off-grid solar power in India
why: A bare connection is not enough; people need enough usable power to change daily life.

authors: Paul Gertler, James Heckman, Rodrigo Pinto, Arianna Zanolini, Christel Vermeersch, Susan Walker, Susan M. Chang, Sally Grantham-McGregor
finding: Two years of weekly home visits for growth stunted toddlers in Jamaica raised their earnings by 25 percent when they were checked 20 years later.
title: Labor market returns to an early childhood stimulation intervention in Jamaica
why: Low cost help for parents in the first years can lift a child out of a lasting earnings gap.

authors: Arthur J. Reynolds, Judy A. Temple, Suh-Ruu Ou, Irma A. Arteaga, Barry A. B. White
finding: By age 28, children from low income Chicago families in the Child-Parent Center program had health insurance coverage of 75.9 percent, compared with 63.9 percent in the comparison group.
title: School-Based Early Childhood Education and Age-28 Well-Being: Effects by Timing, Dosage, and Subgroups
why: A public program run at scale in ordinary schools can still protect health and income well into adult life.

authors: Julianne Holt-Lunstad, Timothy B. Smith, Mark Baker, Tyler Harris, David Stephenson
finding: Across the studies reviewed, loneliness raised the likelihood of death by 26 percent, social isolation by 29 percent, and living alone by 32 percent.
title: Loneliness and Social Isolation as Risk Factors for Mortality: A Meta-Analytic Review
why: Human connection is a basic health need in later life, not a luxury a commons can leave to chance.

authors: Gill Livingston, Jonathan Huntley, Andrew Sommerlad, David Ames, Clive Ballard, and coauthors
finding: Twelve changeable risk factors account for around 40 percent of dementia cases worldwide, so those cases could in theory be prevented or delayed.
title: Dementia prevention, intervention, and care: 2020 report of the Lancet Commission
why: Much of the burden of old age can be cut by shared action on schooling, hearing, blood pressure, clean air, and social contact.

authors: World Health Organization and World Bank
finding: More than 1 billion people lived with a disability, and in OECD countries only 44 percent of people with disabilities were employed, against 75 percent of people without disabilities.
title: World report on disability
venue: World Health Organization and World Bank report
why: A commons that counts a billion people from the start builds its floor wide enough for everyone to stand on it.

authors: Zuyi Fang, Ilan Cerna-Turoff, Cheng Zhang, Mengyao Lu, Jamie M. Lachman, Jane Barlow
finding: Pooling 98 studies, the authors found that 31.7 percent of children with disabilities had experienced violence.
title: Global estimates of violence against children with disabilities: an updated systematic review and meta-analysis
why: Safety comes before learning or work, so protection for the children most at risk has to be part of the floor itself.

authors: Robert Jensen
finding: After mobile phones spread among Kerala fishers, their profits rose by 8 percent and the prices paid by consumers fell by 4 percent.
title: The Digital Provide: Information (Technology), Market Performance, and Welfare in the South Indian Fisheries Sector
why: Cheap access to price information lets poor sellers earn more while poor buyers pay less at the same time.

authors: Tavneet Suri, William Jack
finding: Access to mobile money in Kenya lifted 194,000 households, 2 percent of all households, out of poverty.
title: The long-run poverty and gender impacts of mobile money
why: A basic phone service that moves and stores money safely can cut poverty without a bank branch in place.

authors: Will Dobbie, Jacob Goldin, Crystal S. Yang
finding: Being held for just 3 days before trial raised the probability of a guilty finding by 14 percentage points.
title: The Effects of Pretrial Detention on Conviction, Future Crime, and Employment: Evidence from Randomly Assigned Judges
why: Locking people up before any finding of guilt tilts the case against them and pushes them out of lawful work.

authors: Devah Pager
finding: White test applicants without a criminal record received callbacks for 34 percent of jobs, compared with 17 percent for white applicants with a record.
title: The Mark of a Criminal Record
why: If a past record halves a fair chance at a job, people leaving prison need a real path back to earning a living.

authors: David B. Lobell, Wolfram Schlenker, Justin Costa-Roberts
finding: Climate trends from 1980 to 2008 cut global maize production by 3.8 percent and wheat production by 5.5 percent compared with a world without those trends.
title: Climate Trends and Global Crop Production Since 1980
why: Food sits at the base of human need, so adapting staple crops is one way a commons protects the floor for everyone.

authors: Antonio Gasparrini, Yuming Guo, Masahiro Hashizume, and coauthors
finding: Across 384 locations, 7.71 percent of deaths were linked to temperatures outside the safest range, with cold linked to 7.29 percent and heat to 0.42 percent.
title: Mortality risk attributable to high and low ambient temperature: a multicountry observational study
why: Safe shelter, heating, cooling, and early warnings can prevent deaths that fall hardest on people with the least money and protection.

authors: Abhijit Banerjee, Esther Duflo, Nathanael Goldberg, Dean Karlan, Robert Osei, William Parienté, Jeremy Shapiro, Bram Thuysbaert, Christopher Udry
finding: In trials with 10,495 people in six countries, 8 of 10 outcome measures still showed significant gains one year after the program ended.
title: A multifaceted program causes lasting progress for the very poor: Evidence from six countries
why: Assets, training, coaching, cash support, and savings access given together can help the poorest people build a lasting living that others can copy openly.

authors: Michael A. Clemens, Claudio E. Montenegro, Lant Pritchett
finding: The average price equivalent of migration barriers to the United States for low skill men was more than 13,700 dollars per worker per year.
title: The Place Premium: Bounding the Price Equivalent of Migration Barriers
venue: The Review of Economics and Statistics
why: Fair paths to move for work can lift a family income far more than most help given in place, so birthplace should not lock in poverty.

authors: Jens Hainmueller, Dominik Hangartner, Duncan Lawrence
finding: One extra year of waiting for an asylum decision cut the later employment rate by 4 to 5 percentage points, a drop of 16 to 23 percent from the average rate.
title: When lives are put on hold: Lengthy asylum processes decrease employment among refugees
why: Fast and fair decisions let refugees earn, settle, and contribute sooner instead of losing ground while they wait in limbo.
